candidate.answerReason: The stated tangency to AB at its midpoint produces two unit squares. Each overlap with circle C has area π/2 − 1, so the requested area is π − 2(π/2 − 1) = 2, matching C.

methods.label: Subtract the two equal overlaps
methods.explanation:
The two overlaps are congruent, so we can calculate one and subtract it twice from the area of circle \(C\). Let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(\overline{AB}\). The externally tangent unit circles \(A\) and \(B\) have \(AB=2\), so \(AM=BM=1\). The stated tangency of circle \(C\) to \(\overline{AB}\) at \(M\) gives \(CM=1\) and \(CM\perp AB\). Reflection across \(CM\) exchanges circles \(A\) and \(B\) while leaving circle \(C\) fixed.

[Figure 1](figures/2011_AMC_10A_Q18_question_fig1.svg)

Complete the unit square \(AMCP\). Because \(AP=CP=1\), point \(P\) lies on both circles \(A\) and \(C\). Their entire overlap lies in this square: circle \(A\) extends no farther right than \(M\) or above \(P\), while circle \(C\) extends no farther left than \(P\) or below \(M\).

Inside the square, the two disks occupy quarter-disks centered at opposite corners \(A\) and \(C\). These quarter-disks cover the square. Indeed, the first contains triangle \(AMP\), the second contains triangle \(CMP\), and these triangles fill the square. Each triangle lies inside its quarter-disk because it is bounded by two radii and their joining chord.

Each quarter-disk has area \(\pi/4\). Adding their areas counts the unit square once and their overlap once more. Thus one overlap has area
\[
\frac{\pi}{4}+\frac{\pi}{4}-1
=\frac{\pi}{2}-1.
\]
Circles \(A\) and \(B\) touch at only one point, so the two overlaps have no common area. The requested area is therefore
\[
\pi-2\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-1\right)=\boxed{2},
\]
which is choice \(\text{C}\).
methods.levelReason: Uses elementary tangency geometry, reflection, square area, and quarter-circle areas obtained by dividing a full circle into four equal pieces.

methods.label: Rearrange the region into a rectangle
methods.explanation:
We can move the curved pieces to form a rectangle. Let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(\overline{AB}\). Since the unit circles \(A\) and \(B\) touch externally, \(AM=BM=1\). Circle \(C\) is tangent to \(\overline{AB}\) at \(M\), so \(CM=1\) and \(CM\perp AB\).

Complete the unit squares \(AMCP\) and \(MBQC\). Together they form rectangle \(ABQP\), whose width is \(2\) and height is \(1\). Points \(P,C,Q\) lie on its top edge. The lower semicircle of circle \(C\) lies in this rectangle. Its upper semicircle is entirely outside circles \(A\) and \(B\), which rise only to line \(PQ\).

Within the rectangle, circle \(A\) occupies the quarter-disk centered at \(A\), and circle \(B\) occupies the quarter-disk centered at \(B\). Every point outside these quarter-disks belongs to circle \(C\). To see why, diagonal \(MP\) divides the left square into triangle \(AMP\), contained in disk \(A\), and triangle \(MCP\), contained in disk \(C\). Diagonal \(MQ\) gives the corresponding division of the right square into triangles contained in disks \(B\) and \(C\). Thus the desired lower portion is exactly the rectangle with those two quarter-disks removed.

Now divide the upper semicircle of \(C\) into its left and right quarters. Translate the right quarter so that its center moves from \(C\) to \(A\); it fills the missing quarter-disk at \(A\). Translate the left quarter so that its center moves from \(C\) to \(B\); it fills the missing quarter-disk at \(B\). The pieces fill the rectangle without gaps or overlapping interiors.

Translation preserves area, so the requested area is
\[
2\cdot1=\boxed{2},
\]
choice \(\text{C}\).
methods.levelReason: Uses only unit squares, elementary circle geometry, and area-preserving translations. No formula for curved area is needed.

review.mathematicalCheck: The depicted tangency gives AM=BM=CM=1 and CM perpendicular to AB. The opposite quarter-disks cover each unit square, giving each overlap area π/2−1. Subtracting both overlaps gives π−2(π/2−1)=2. The second method's specified translations correctly fill the missing quarter-disks and produce a 2 by 1 rectangle.
